summary: For 10-11 year olds, this is the capstone of mathematical modelling: choosing a fit-for-purpose tool (bar model, double number line, ratio table, labelled 3D diagram + volume formula, scale factor), computing, and then making the decisive judgement — does this answer need rounding, which way, and to what accuracy, and does the SITUATION rather than a rote rule decide? The anchor case is the bus problem (328 people, 40-seat coaches → 8.2 → you must book 9), where the 'exact' decimal is the wrong real answer. Core activities put the child in authentic decisions where naive rounding visibly fails, kept alongside spatial volume work and a dialogue variant that presses for a committed, justified answer.
misconceptions: Reports the bare quotient (8.2 buses) and never rounds to the whole buses the situation demands, or rounds the wrong way (down) leaving people stranded
Rounds by rote to the nearest whole/decimal place regardless of what the context needs (money to 2 dp, buses always UP, lengths to sensible precision)
Reasons additively about ratio/scale (adds the same amount to both quantities) instead of multiplicatively
Blurs volume with area or length, or reports cm³ answers in the wrong unit
Chooses a tool by habit (single bar) that hides the two covarying quantities in a rate/ratio problem

activities.title: Order the coaches: when 8.2 is the wrong answer
steps: Take the real job: 328 people need to travel to a match; each coach seats 40. Build a ratio table or double number line, or divide, and land on 8.2.
Make the rounding decision explicitly: do I round? which way? to what accuracy? and WHY — state the reason before trusting the number.
Check the consequence of rounding down: 8 coaches × 40 = 320 seats, leaving 8 people with no seat. Commit to 9 coaches and justify it by those stranded people.
Explain in your own words why the SITUATION (a coach is indivisible, nobody can be left behind) decides the direction, not the nearest-whole rule.
Try the exact-division contrast: if only 320 people travelled, 320 ÷ 40 = 8 exactly, so no rounding decision arises — notice the dilemma only appears when the division leaves a remainder.

Try a variant that rounds the OTHER way: 'how many FULL crates can we pack from 328 apples, 40 to a crate?' — here you round down to 8 full crates (8 apples left over). Explain why the direction differs.
activities.insight: A computed decimal must be interpreted back against the real question; whether and which way to round is a judgement the context makes, not a rule applied on autopilot. The same arithmetic rounds up for coaches and down for full crates, and when the division is exact (320 ÷ 40 = 8) there is no rounding decision at all.

activities.title: Choosing the right tool for a proportional problem
steps: Before computing, pick a tool that matches the structure: double number line or ratio table for ratio/rate, bar model for part-whole ratio and comparison, scale factor for similar shapes.
Set up a ratio/scale problem and keep BOTH covarying quantities visible — e.g. on a double number line label litres against cost, or recipe quantities against servings.
Scale multiplicatively, not additively: check that if one quantity is multiplied by a factor, the other is multiplied by the same factor, rather than adding the same amount to both.
Explain why a single bar that shows only one quantity would hide the rate, and choose a tool that doesn't.
activities.insight: Proportional situations covary multiplicatively; choosing a representation that keeps both quantities in view prevents the common additive error and sets up a correct model before any rounding question arises.

activities.title: Volume as capacity: pack it, compute it, then decide the accuracy
steps: Pack a box or tank with unit cubes to feel volume as capacity, then connect this to the formula V = l×w×h (or V = base area × height).
Compute the volume of a labelled container and keep units alive: distinguish cm (length), cm² (area) and cm³ (volume), and report the answer in the right unit.
Answer a real decision that forces rounding the correct way, e.g. 'how many full crates fit inside?' (round down) or 'will this tank overflow if we pour in X litres?'.

For a measurement like a tank holding 12.7 litres, decide to what accuracy you should state it and say who or what in the situation decides that precision (note: 12.7 is an illustrative figure, not computed from given dimensions).
activities.insight: Volume is a real capacity, not just a formula output; units must be tracked (cm³ ≠ cm² ≠ cm), and the required precision and rounding direction depend on the physical situation (not overflowing, counting only full containers).

activities.title: Defend your answer to the client (spoken variant)
steps: Role-play with an event organiser or engineer who presses for a real decision: 'The maths said 8.2 — do I book 8 or 9? What happens to the other people?'
Commit to a whole, bookable answer and defend the direction of rounding out loud by naming the consequence.
Handle a sprung variant that tests transfer, e.g. 330 people with 44-seat coaches (330 ÷ 44 = 7.5 → 8 coaches), or a round-down full-boxes case, and justify the new decision.
Respond to the challenge 'you always round up in word problems — true?' with a counter-example where rounding up would be wrong.
activities.insight: Being able to commit to and justify a context-appropriate rounded answer in dialogue — and to say when 'always round up' fails — shows the judgement is situation-driven, not a memorised rule.

activities.title: Sub-skill checks feeding the real task
steps: Practise isolated sub-skills on short items: compute a volume from a labelled diagram, simplify a ratio, or complete a row of a ratio table.
Immediately feed each checked sub-skill back into a full modelling task that requires the rounding-in-context decision, rather than stopping at the computed number.
activities.insight: Fluency with the component operations supports, but does not replace, the modelling judgement; a correct computation is only the start of answering the real question.

checkQuestion: 328 people need to travel to a match. Each coach holds 40 people. A pupil divides and gets 8.2, and writes '8.2 coaches'. Is that the answer the organiser needs? Talk me through what you'd actually tell them to book, and why.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that 8.2 coaches is not a bookable quantity, that you must round UP to 9 (8 coaches leaves 8 people with no seat), and that the SITUATION, not a rounding rule, decides the direction. A child who accepts '8.2', or who rounds to 8 'because .2 rounds down', has computed correctly but not modelled — they haven't interpreted the result against the real question.
